title: Sally Rooney says her books will be removed from sale in UK over Palestine Action support
description: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Act
body: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK."I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work."To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza.In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. "The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested.On Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence."After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced".Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action".More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action.About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month.

schema.headline: Sally Rooney says her books will be removed from sale in UK over Palestine Action support

title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
description: Figure caption, Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham mattersByKate Whannel Political reporterUpdated 3 hours ago"We are behind you and that will not ch
body: Figure caption, Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham mattersByKate Whannel Political reporterUpdated 3 hours ago"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street. Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones. Ukrainian officials have said that overnight strikes by Russian missiles and drones had left at least 600,000 people without electricity. For the second consecutive night, Ukraine said it had not received advanced warning from its allies of a wave of missile strikes coming from Russia.Zelensky has suggested the US had threatened to restrict intelligence-sharing unless he agreed to sign up to an energy ceasefire. Trump has denied the US is holding back information. An adviser to the president has also said Ukraine's ability to defend itself from incoming missiles has been hindered by disruptions to its connection with the Starlink internet network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.Serhiy Beskrestnov said the move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.Speaking in Downing Street, Burnham said the recent days had been "dark and difficult" for Ukraine, with the country suffering "heavy bombardment".He told the Ukrainian leader: "You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain."We are behind you and that will not change."Image source, PA MediaEarlier in the day, Burnham had been invited to criticise the US decision to lift sanctions on Russia, when, at Prime Minister's Questions, Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey asked if the PM agreed there had been a "shameful Trump betrayal". Burnham acknowledged that Zelensky was "carrying the heaviest of weights" but avoided attacking Trump, instead telling MPs that his role was to "repair bridges so that the support comes back"."Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."He added that Zelensky would not come away from his trip "empty-handed". In a statement following the meeting, a Downing Street spokeswoman said the leaders had discussed "Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure".She said the prime minister promised that the UK would continue to develop "innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The King held an audience with President Zelensky at Buckingham Palace as part of his visit to the UKOn Friday, Trump shocked European allies when he announced that he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel, with more to follow. Concerns about the cost of living are playing a key part in the US's November elections and the US president hopes his deal with Russia will reduce the cost of diesel. The agreement runs counter to sanctions imposed on Russia by the US and its allies in a bid to choke off funds for Putin's war in Ukraine.The deal came days after Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" and that it was time for Ukraine to "get a new president".The criticism marks a renewal of Trump's previous hostility towards Zelensky which resulted in an infamous public row between the two men in the Oval Office.

schema.headline: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky

title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
description: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the wom
body: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred"."His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court.The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return".But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met".The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters.She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened".On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences.The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told.She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her.The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident".He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity".The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her.She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm.She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on."The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004.Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told.The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets.The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard."He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal."The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999."He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far."Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

schema.headline: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins

title: UK threatens visa bans for Eritrea over migrant return policy
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment."Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission. The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of  Congo (DRC).Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

schema.headline: UK threatens visa bans for Eritrea over migrant return policy

title: Airport drop-off charges to be reviewed after sharp increase
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySimon Browning Transport reporterAirport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price incre
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySimon Browning Transport reporterAirport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".'Rip-off' The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers"."We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport."Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports.She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution".The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports.Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households.Get in touchHave you been affected by issues covered in this story?  Share your experiences.

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
description: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by
body: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

schema.headline: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices

title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
description: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined
body: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City."This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

schema.headline: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show

title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
description: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast und
body: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total. Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites". Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples." Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all". "I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting". The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

schema.headline: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments

title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
description: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly
body: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau."Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

schema.headline: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022

title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn thanks prime minister as brain cancer review announced
description: Figure caption, Archie Goodburn said he 'couldn't ask for much more' at this stage of his cancer research pleaByKaty Scott and Claire ThomsonBBC Scotl
body: Figure caption, Archie Goodburn said he 'couldn't ask for much more' at this stage of his cancer research pleaByKaty Scott and Claire ThomsonBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoSwimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner. Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else. "Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.The review will be led Prof Anthony Chalmers, who is chairman of clinical oncology at the University of Glasgow, and will assess what progress has been made in the sector since 2018.It aims to highlight "what is still holding progress back".This will be followed by a national cancer plan with a view to get new treatments "out of the lab and to patients faster," Downing Street said. It added the prime minister has asked the medicines regulator, the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), to conclude its review of the rules for medicines that treat rare conditions sooner.He has urged the regulator to complete the review in two years rather than three, bringing forward any changes to the rules that could help patients get new treatments sooner. Speaking on BBC Breakfast earlier this year, Goodburn described how trials around the world are not being seen in the UK which is "unfair and unjust".The government added that patients, families and charities will help design a drive to get more people onto clinical trials.Health Secretary Yvette Cooper, who also attended the meeting in Downing Street, is set to lead it.Figure caption, Watch Archie Goodburn's emotional plea for more brain cancer funding on BBC BreakfastFollowing the meeting, Goodburn said: "They have listened to the thousands of voices all around the country and the thousands of families who have been begging for change for years."All three asks have been promised to some extent and there is some fleshing out that needs to be done on the details."I don't think I could ask for much more at this point so I sent a very strong thanks to Andy Burnham for his time."A spokesperson for the UK government said the announcement applies to the whole of the United Kingdom as the research body involved - the National Institute for Health and Social Care Research (NIHR) - works in collaboration with devolved administrations in a number of its funding programmes.Health and social services are a devolved power in Scotland.First Minister John Swinney, who also recently met Goodburn, noted the Scottish government's commitment to support more clinical trials.He said: "We are proud to support national leadership for brain cancer through the Scottish Adult Neuro-Oncology Network. "This brings together clinicians, patients and voluntary sector representatives to improve the care of people with brain cancers across Scotland."We will give careful consideration to any further role which Scotland could play to give people living with brain cancer a faster route from research to treatment."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Archie Goodburn was diagnosed with three oligodendroglioma tumours in 2024Charity Brain Tumour Research said the disease was the cancer most likely to kill patients under 40 in the UK.They said charities made up more than 75% of the total national investment in brain tumour research, with the government funding sitting at 25%.Following the announcement, chief executive Dan Knowles thanked Goodburn for his "tireless efforts" in raising awareness of the disease.He said: "We are optimistic that this renewed focus will help ensure discoveries in the laboratory actually make it to patients who so desperately need more options."The Rare Cancers Bill, led by Edinburgh South West MP Scott Arthur, became law earlier this year.The legislation aims to incentivise research and investment into the treatment of rare types of cancer, defined as those affecting fewer than 1 in every 2,000 people.But Goodburn previously said that did not go far enough and a dedicated brain cancer lead would allow for greater focus on specific research and trials.Arthur said the act was "vital" to driving research needed into the condition, but Goodburn's meeting with Burnham could lead to further work in the field."There is real opportunity in the sector to dismantle the barriers to research that charities, clinicians, and researchers have known about for decades," he said before the meeting."Having met Archie a number of times I know he is a fantastic advocate for the brain tumour community."I hope his meeting with the prime minister is a moment for concrete progress to be made."

schema.headline: Swimmer Archie Goodburn thanks prime minister as brain cancer review announced

title: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
description: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connecte
body: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said."Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".The US government has not commented.While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities. Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel."Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones."We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

schema.headline: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds

title: Bradley Barcola arrives in style as Liverpool beat LASK in Champions League
description: On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.Given
body: On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.Given their price tags, the pressure was on both to start delivering after stuttering starts to their individual campaigns. Iraola, as most managers would, stood by his players, insisting he trusted them "100%". Iraola insisted the focus was on the collective rather than individual stats but there is no denying that when you spend such eye-watering sums - £116m on Wirtz and £123m on Barcola - you want those players to be match-winners.Wirtz delivered a fine display in the Austrian city of Linz as Liverpool won 6-3, with an assist to show for his efforts. However, this was a night where the headlines belonged to Barcola, who on the 238th appearance of his career across clubs and country combined, scored his first hat-trick.And it was those three goals which proved to be the difference as Liverpool returned to winning ways after their 3-0 loss to Manchester City on Sunday. In truth, the 24-year-old could have scored more such was his quality, but he did enough to take the match ball home after two fine finishes with his right foot and left foot, followed by a tap in after the break.And a little over 24 hours after defending his players against  those pre-match questions, Iraola was speaking with a smile on his face. "I'm really happy for Bradley," Iraola said."You were asking me yesterday about him not making the numbers and [the same with] Florian and I think both of them today played really, really well. I think they made a difference."Bradley was a threat, always when one-on-one [and] certainly in behind. He helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am and happy for both of them."I think for their confidence it's very good.  I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. I think it's going to be very good, very good for them."On what it could mean for Barcola, Iraola added: "I think he has to enjoy this [as] to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult. "Even yesterday in training, I could feel he was very lively. Sometimes you feel these things [are going to happen]. We were feeling he was in a good place going into the game."Barcola will now hope to show that level in the Premier League, starting with a visit to Brentford on Saturday.Iraola's side were relentless in the first-half against the Austrian Bundesliga champions, racing into a three-goal lead. Such was their dominance, they could have easily scored more.The 19 shots Liverpool had by half time against LASK was the most on record since 2003-04 by any team in the first half of a Champions League away match. If there was any criticism, it would be that they were guilty of becoming a little complacent in the second half, conceding three goals after the hour mark but in fairness, the job was all but done.There were more positives to take on the night, with both full-backs coming into the side and performing well. Jeremie Frimpong scored and registered two assists while Kostas Tsimikas added two assists of his own. Ronald Araujo also scored his first goal for the club since joining in the summer and Lewis Koumas got no less than he deserved when he got on the scoresheet in the second half. The 21-year-old even had two goals ruled out for offside but his first-half assist for Barcola meant that he became the youngster player to score and assist in a  Champions League match for Liverpool (21y 25d), with the previous youngest being Steven Gerrard (21y 139d v Dynamo Kyiv in 2001). Fine company, indeed.But Liverpool will know that they won’t get many easier games than this over the course of the season. LASK came into this game, winless in their last four matches.“What do you take from that? It's very difficult because the game was very passive for large periods,” said Stephen Warnock on 5 Live.”There were parts where I am watching Trey Nyoni in midfield and he has literally got no pressure on him at all, he is picking passes off.“Barcola has got the run of his full-back who was taken off at half-time, which tells you everything.“I don't read too much into it, because I expected Liverpool to go there and win, and win comfortably."Warnock added that a bigger test for Liverpool will come at Brentford on Saturday, the Bees fourth in the table and unbeaten in the league.“Can Barcola do that again, away at Brentford, because that is what they have essentially bought him for, to play in big games away from home," Warnock said.“He hasn't played that much football this season so [this game] was about getting minutes in his legs and getting him fit and getting him sharper. The acid test will be Brentford away.”

schema.headline: Bradley Barcola arrives in style as Liverpool beat LASK in Champions League

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
description: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporea
body: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says

title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic t
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000)."Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a  shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clockmaking shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day."Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.The grainy footage, which has no audio, shows her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.Clarkson can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store treated her rudely came as a surprise.Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here."I really like it here."

schema.headline: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
description: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air f
body: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and  Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
